newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - France, peripherals shine at short end.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - France, peripherals shine at short end.

text.p: Short-end bond investors can profit from a post-Dublin glow of confidence about European Economic and Monetary Union by anticipating interest rate cuts in France and peripheral markets, analysts said on Wednesday.
They said the European Union summit last week had made a timely start to EMU more likely and this was underpinning newfound confidence, especially by the Bank of France.
"The best value in any short end is really in France," said Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Europe.

"Of all the continental European countries it has the most scope to cut rates where this has not already been discounted," he added, comparing it with Italy where markets expected 150 basis points to come off official rates by spring.

Sonia Gibbs, bond strategist at Nomura International, however, said peripheral Europe still afforded the best money-making prospects for short-end bond investors in the immediate future, provided they could stomach the risk.
"France is a small but almost certain gain as opposed to a probably very large but much less certain gain in Italy and Spain," she said.

Jessop predicted France would whittle its intervention rate down 15 basis points from 3.15 percent currently, in order to match the 3.00 percent repo rate in Germany. It would also follow the Bundesbank in lopping what he predicted would be 50 basis points off interest rates in the next few months.
Gibbs said the Dublin stability pact, to ensure budgetary discipline by member states post-EMU, meant there was even less justification now for a French bond premium over Germany.
She said the French yield spread versus Germany on two-year bonds had "scope to go distinctly negative". The two-year spread was about three b.p. at 1500 GMT, against 40 b.p in mid-October.
Gibbs agreed that France, which shaved five basis points off the intervention rate on Tuesday, would cut the remaining 10 to 15 basis points to get flat with Germany.

Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London, said the Bank of France could probably close the gap on the German repo rate next year without harming the franc -- unless France's economy looked much weaker than Germany's.
Jessop nominated France as the continental European bond market whose short end merited close investor attention in coming months -- whereas Italy was one to avoid.
Not only were rate cuts discounted in the Italian market, but he said the Bank of Italy might drag its feet, looking to commercial banks to cut rates without it doing more itself.

Throw in the risk of a political crisis early next year that could spark a fall in the lira, and Jessop's conclusion was "risk for disappointment in the short end in Italy but some pleasant surprises in France".
Gibbs said the present wave of EMU optimism was likely to continue to buoy European bonds in the early months of 1997.

"Only when you get into the mini-budget season and examination of 1998 budgets will you see concerns," she said, adding that Italy would have little leeway then to react to any budget overshoot without tumbling into recession.
Reed said Italy had more scope than countries like Spain and Sweden for rate easing independent of the Bundesbank. She cited growing inflationary pressures albeit from a low base in Sweden.
She said German bonds were fairly priced at the short end, and should be considered by prudent investors in the German market concerned about the implications of EMU for longer bonds.
"They should probably think about the short end, not that there is a lot to be gained there but there is a lot less to be lost," Reed said.
